claims.source: Overexpression of the related enzymes ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 both markedly enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at the expense of cytosolic NLRP3 signal, with ZDHHC3 having a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: ZDHHC3 has a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
claims.source: Overexpression of the related enzymes ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 both markedly enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at the expense of cytosolic NLRP3 signal, with ZDHHC3 having a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: ZDHHC2, ZDHHC8 and ZDHHC9 weakly enhance NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
claims.source: To a much weaker extent, ZDHHC2, ZDHHC8 and ZDHHC9 also enhanced NLRP3 Golgi recruitment (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of ZDHHC5 causes NLRP3 to re-localise to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, overexpression of the plasma membrane localised PAT ZDHHC5 decreased the amount of NLRP3 at the Golgi and instead caused NLRP3 to re-localise to the plasma membrane (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The effect of ZDHHC overexpression on NLRP3 localisation is dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
claims.source: The effect of ZDHHC overexpression on NLRP3 localisation was dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzyme as catalytically inactive ZDHHC3C157S had no effect on recruitment on NLRP3 to the Golgi (Figure 2E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claims.claim: Cys-130 is essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
claims.source: Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 were both essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment and the effect of ZDHHC5 on recruitment of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane as mutating either of these features prevented NLRP3 re-localisation in response to ZDHHC overexpression (Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claims.claim: Hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 are essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
claims.source: Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 were both essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment and the effect of ZDHHC5 on recruitment of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane as mutating either of these features prevented NLRP3 re-localisation in response to ZDHHC overexpression (Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claims.claim: Sensitivity to plasma membrane localised ZDHHC5 requires an intact PB region.
claims.source: In agreement with the polybasic region driving affinity for highly charged membranes such as the plasma membrane and TGN (Eisenberg et al., 2021), sensitivity to PM localised ZDHHC5 required an intact PB region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Cis-Golgi localised ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 when the PB region is mutated.
claims.source: however, cis-Golgi localised ZDHHC3 (Ernst et al., 2018) was still able to recruit NLRP3 when the PB region was mutated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: Helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of interaction with intracellular membranes independent of the polybasic region.
claims.source: These results suggest that helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of interaction with intracellular membranes independent of the polybasic region, likely through the hydrophobic residues within helix115-125, but not at sufficient levels to show noticeable enrichment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 with mutated PB region.

claims.claim: Endogenous NLRP3 localises to the perinuclear region where it partially overlaps with the trans-Golgi marker p230 in THP-1 cells.
claims.source: As previously described (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018), endogenous NLRP3 localised to the perinuclear region where it partially overlapped with the trans-Golgi marker p230 (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior work (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018).

claims.claim: Mutation of Cys-130 removes the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the requirement for Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues for Golgi localisation in HeLaM cells, mutation of these residues removed the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 (Figure 3B and C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: Mutation of hydrophobic residues preceding Cys-130 removes the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the requirement for Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues for Golgi localisation in HeLaM cells, mutation of these residues removed the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 (Figure 3B and C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhances Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
claims.source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S markedly enhances the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment in THP-1 cells.
claims.source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E) and markedly enhanced the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment (Figure 3F and G)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: Higher levels of ZDHHC3 activity can induce a greater percentage of cells to undergo NLRP3-dependent cell death.
claims.source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E) and markedly enhanced the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment (Figure 3F and G), demonstrating that higher levels of ZDHHC3 activity can induce a greater percentage of cells to undergo NLRP3-dependent cell death.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: Labelling of S-acylated cysteines in NLRP3 reveals two bands indicative of singly and doubly S-acylated NLRP3 species in both HeLaM and THP1 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the presence of multiple cysteines in NLRP3 being S-acylated, labelling of S-acylated cysteines in NLRP3 revealed two bands indicative of singly and doubly S-acylated NLRP3 species in both HeLaM and THP1 cells (Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: A large amount of NLRP3 remains resistant to hydroxylamine, suggesting a significant proportion of NLRP3 is not S-acylated at steady state.
claims.source: A large amount of NLRP3 remained resistant to hydroxylamine, suggesting a significant proportion of NLRP3 is not S-acylated at steady state.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: Mutation of Cys-130 leads to only subtle changes in the S-acylation profile of NLRP3 with no loss of doubly S-acylated NLRP3.
claims.source: Surprisingly, mutation of Cys-130 led to only subtle changes in the S-acylation profile of NLRP3 with no loss of doubly S-acylated NLRP3 (Figure 4A and C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claims.claim: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression correlates with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species.
claims.source: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression and nigericin treatment both correlated with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species which did not occur when Cys-130 was mutated (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment correlates with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species.
claims.source: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression and nigericin treatment both correlated with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species which did not occur when Cys-130 was mutated (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: GFP-NLRP395-158 displays no mass shift following labelling of exposed S-acylated cysteines at steady state.
claims.source: GFP-NLRP395-158 displayed no mass shift following labelling of exposed S-acylated cysteines and did not localise to the Golgi (Figure 4E–G), indicating that in the context of the small peptide used for this experiment, Cys-130 is not significantly S-acylated at steady state.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increases enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi.
claims.source: However, overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increased enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi (Figure 4E and F)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 induces a mass shift of NLRP395-158 following 5 kDa PEG maleimide labelling that is dependent on Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues.
claims.source: However, overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increased enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi (Figure 4E and F) and induced a mass shift of NLRP395-158 following 5 kDa PEG maleimide labelling that was dependent on Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The linker region preceding the PB region is capable of undergoing S-acylation at Cys-130.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that the linker region preceding the PB region is capable of undergoing S-acylation at Cys-130.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the PEG-switch assay data showing Cys-130 dependent mass shift in NLRP395-158 upon ZDHHC3 overexpression (Figure 4G).

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB causes loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi.
claims.source: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB had a similar effect on NLRP3, with loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi (Figure 5A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB causes re-localisation of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane, tubular recycling endosomes, and late endosomes.
claims.source: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB had a similar effect on NLRP3, with loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi (Figure 5A) and re-localisation of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane, tubular recycling endosomes, and late endosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 significantly reduces localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells.
claims.source: Consistent with NLRP3 undergoing de-acylation, overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 (Abrami et al., 2021), but not mitochondrially localised APT1 (Kathayat et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), significantly reduced localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of mitochondrially localised APT1 does not significantly reduce localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells.
claims.source: Consistent with NLRP3 undergoing de-acylation, overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 (Abrami et al., 2021), but not mitochondrially localised APT1 (Kathayat et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), significantly reduced localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Overexpressed APT2 has no impact on Golgi morphology.
claims.source: Overexpressed APT2 had no impact on Golgi morphology, indicating that loss of NLRP3 from Golgi membranes was not due to an effect of excess APT2 on Golgi integrity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–J.

claims.claim: PalmostatinB treatment limits the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin.
claims.source: Both PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression also limited the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin (Figure 5C and D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: APT2 overexpression limits the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin.
claims.source: Both PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression also limited the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin (Figure 5C and D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial re-routing of APT2 from the Golgi prior to nigericin stimulation restores the enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi observed in response to nigericin.
claims.source: The effect of APT2 overexpression appeared to be acute, suggestive of a direct action on NLRP3, as mitochondrial re-routing of APT2 from the Golgi prior to nigericin stimulation restored the enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi observed in response to nigericin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–G.

claims.claim: NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle.
claims.source: Thus, NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined effects of PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression on NLRP3 localization.

claims.claim: The kinetics of NLRP3 membrane binding in untreated cells are similar to those described for mono-S-acylated N-Ras with a half time to recovery of 58.4 s (±9.3 s S.D.).
claims.source: The kinetics of NLRP3 membrane binding in untreated cells were similar to those described for mono-S-acylated N-Ras (Rocks et al., 2005) with a half time to recovery of 58.4 s (±9.3 ss S.D.), in agreement with NLRP3 rapidly cycling on and off the Golgi in an S-acylation cycle (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5E and F and citation to prior work (Rocks et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment suppresses the fluorescence recovery of NLRP3 after photobleaching.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment suppressed the fluorescence recovery; whilst GFP-NLRP3 signal on average recovered to 75% of the pre-bleach signal in untreated cells, this was reduced to 44% after nigericin treatment, indicating that a greater fraction of NLRP3 that makes up the signal in the Golgi region is immobile following nigericin treatment (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: A greater fraction of NLRP3 is immobile following nigericin treatment.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment suppressed the fluorescence recovery; whilst GFP-NLRP3 signal on average recovered to 75% of the pre-bleach signal in untreated cells, this was reduced to 44% after nigericin treatment, indicating that a greater fraction of NLRP3 that makes up the signal in the Golgi region is immobile following nigericin treatment (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: A proportion of perinuclear NLRP3 in nigericin treated cells remains resistant to rapamycin induced mitochondrial re-routing.
claims.source: Reduced mobility of Golgi localised NLRP3 by FRAP was consistent with a mitochondrial re-routing assay using FKBP tagged GFP-NLRP3 where a proportion of perinuclear NLRP3 in nigericin treated cells remained resistant to rapamycin induced mitochondrial re-routing (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial re-routing assay data shown in Figure 5H, I.

claims.claim: Changes in the membrane binding cycle of NLRP3 accompany its activation.
claims.source: Changes in the membrane binding cycle of NLRP3 therefore accompany its activation, with less NLRP3 cycling off Golgi membranes following nigericin treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from FRAP and mitochondrial re-routing data showing reduced NLRP3 mobility after nigericin treatment.

claims.claim: APT2 is tethered to the cytoplasmic face of the Golgi via S-acylation by the cis-Golgi localised PATs ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7.
claims.source: The thioesterase enzyme APT2 is known to reside at the Golgi and is tethered to its cytoplasmic face via S-acylation by the cis-Golgi localised PATs ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 (Abrami et al., 2021; Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Ernst et al., 2018; Lin and Conibear, 2015; Vartak et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Abrami et al., 2021; Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Ernst et al., 2018; Lin and Conibear, 2015; Vartak et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In untreated cells, APT2S122A and NLRP3 signal are closely opposed.
claims.source: In untreated cells, APT2S122A and NLRP3 signal were closely opposed (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: After nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulates on structures that are largely devoid of APT2S122A.
claims.source: However, whilst some NLRP3 signal overlapped with APT2S122A after nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulated on structures that were largely devoid of APT2S122A (Figure 6A and B) indicating that APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
claims.source: However, whilst some NLRP3 signal overlapped with APT2S122A after nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulated on structures that were largely devoid of APT2S122A (Figure 6A and B) indicating that APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment induces dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi.
claims.source: In contrast, nigericin treatment induced dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi (Figure 6C), as previously described (Chen and Chen, 2018)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and citation to prior work (Chen and Chen, 2018).

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment induces a less pronounced dissociation of p230 positive trans-Golgi membranes from the cis / medial Golgi.
claims.source: In contrast, nigericin treatment induced dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi (Figure 6C), as previously described (Chen and Chen, 2018), with a less pronounced dissociation of p230 positive trans-Golgi membranes from the cis / medial Golgi also observed (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment leads to significant alterations in the organisation of distal Golgi cisternae relative to proximal cisternae.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment therefore leads to significant alterations in the organisation of distal Golgi cisternae relative to proximal cisternae.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from microscopy data showing dissociation of TGN and trans-Golgi from cis/medial Golgi (Figure 6C-D).

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin inhibits trafficking of FM4-hGH through the Golgi.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claims.claim: Nigericin treatment has no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claims.claim: Golgi secretion and the flow of material beyond cis- and medial-Golgi cisternae is impaired by nigericin.
claims.source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F), demonstrating that Golgi secretion and the flow of material beyond cis- and medial-Golgi cisternae is impaired by nigericin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM4-hGH trafficking data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claims.claim: Disruptions to Golgi organisation and function caused by nigericin may limit the ability of APT2 to come into contact with NLRP3 and de-acylate it.
claims.source: Thus, disruptions to Golgi organisation and function caused by nigericin may limit the ability of APT2 to come into contact with NLRP3 and de-acylate it (Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of Golgi disorganization, impaired trafficking, and segregation of APT2 from NLRP3.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells with monensin causes NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi.
claims.source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H.

claims.claim: Monensin does not activate NLRP3.
claims.source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992).

claims.claim: Monensin impairs Golgi function.
claims.source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H) and impaired Golgi function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FM4-hGH trafficking data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The NLRP3 polybasic region alone is insufficient to achieve localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi.
claims.source: NLRP3 Golgi binding has to date been shown to require interactions between the polybasic region of NLRP3 and PI4P (Chen and Chen, 2018). The NLRP3 polybasic region alone, however, is insufficient to achieve localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that GFP-NLRP3131-158 does not localize to the Golgi (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: Electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction.
claims.source: Similar to other peripheral membrane proteins that are S-acylated (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008), electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes provided by S-acylation at Cys-130 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and comparison to other S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins, supported by citations (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes is provided by S-acylation at Cys-130.
claims.source: Similar to other peripheral membrane proteins that are S-acylated (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008), electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes provided by S-acylation at Cys-130 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutation of Cys-130 prevents Golgi enrichment.

claims.claim: Cys-130, helix115-125 and the polybasic region form a highly conserved functional unit that are essential for localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi apparatus.
claims.source: Collectively, Cys-130, helix115-125 and the polybasic region form a highly conserved functional unit that are essential for localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi apparatus and potentially other intracellular membranes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined mutagenesis data showing that all three features are required for Golgi localization.

claims.claim: LRR-dependent formation of an oligomeric NLRP3 complex may increase affinity for intracellular membranes through an avidity-based effect.
claims.source: LRR-dependent formation of an oligomeric NLRP3 complex may therefore increase affinity for intracellular membranes through an avidity-based effect dependent on multiple monomers working together within a larger NLRP3 oligomer.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that the LRR domain enhances Golgi binding and from structural data showing polybasic regions organized around Cys-130.

claims.claim: ZDHHC7 is responsible for NLRP3 S-acylation at Cys-130 in macrophages.
claims.source: In agreement with our results showing that localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi can be controlled by the levels of ZDHHC3/7, a recent pre-print demonstrated that knockout of ZDHHC7 prevents localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi and limits NLRP3 activation, suggesting that ZDHHC7 is responsible for NLRP3 S-acylation at Cys-130 in macrophages (Yu et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent pre-print (Yu et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Alterations in the levels of charged lipids on endosomes caused by NLRP3 stimuli could potentially allow NLRP3 to visit endosomal membranes and be trapped there by an endosomally localised PAT.
claims.source: Alterations in the levels of charged lipids on endosomes caused by NLRP3 stimuli, as has previously been described (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), could potentially allow NLRP3 to visit endosomal membranes and be trapped there by an endosomally localised PAT.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from prior work (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) and the authors' own data on ZDHHC5.

claims.claim: Regulation of access to the Golgi through S-acylation at Cys-130 is likely to be important for oligomer formation.
claims.source: Regulation of access to the Golgi through S-acylation at Cys-130 is likely to be important for oligomer formation and may represent another aspect of regulatory control over NLRP3 activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the known importance of membrane binding for oligomer formation and the authors' data on S-acylation.

claims.claim: The steady state balance of S-acylation and de-acylation at Cys-130 may keep levels of Golgi localised NLRP3 below a critical threshold required for further NLRP3 oligomerisation or access to interaction partners and post translational modifications needed for optimal activation.
claims.source: The steady state balance of S-acylation and de-acylation at Cys-130 may keep levels of Golgi localised NLRP3 below a critical threshold required for further NLRP3 oligomerisation or access to interaction partners and post translational modifications needed for optimal activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the authors' data on the S-acylation cycle.

claims.claim: Deletion of residues 92–120 in mouse NLRP3 impairs IL1β release.
claims.source: In mice, deletion of residues 92–120, which removes part of helix115-125, impairs IL1β release, with longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) completely removing Cys-130 and helix115-125 producing an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) in mouse NLRP3 that completely remove Cys-130 and helix115-125 produce an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation.
claims.source: In mice, deletion of residues 92–120, which removes part of helix115-125, impairs IL1β release, with longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) completely removing Cys-130 and helix115-125 producing an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Deletion of exon-3 (spanning residues 95–134) from human NLRP3 delays but does not completely block NLRP3 activation in human macrophages.
claims.source: In contrast, deletion of exon-3 (spanning residues 95–134) from human NLRP3 delays but does not completely block NLRP3 activation in human macrophages (Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023).

claims.claim: S-acylation at Cys-130 and binding to the Golgi may accelerate the process of inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to NLRP3 agonists.

claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that human NLRP3 can be activated without Golgi binding.

claims.claim: Activation of human NLRP3 can still seemingly occur in the absence of Golgi binding.
claims.source: In light of the latter study, S-acylation at Cys-130 and binding to the Golgi may accelerate the process of inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to NLRP3 agonists, although activation of human NLRP3 can still seemingly occur in the absence of Golgi binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the study by Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023 showing that deletion of exon-3 delays but does not block NLRP3 activation.

results.result: NLRP3 membrane association at the Golgi is critically dependent on S-acylation at Cys-130. Treatment with the S-acylation inhibitor 2-bromopalmitate (2-BP) or mutation of Cys-130 prevents Golgi enrichment of NLRP3 at steady state and in response to nigericin, without affecting Golgi PI4P levels or overall Golgi integrity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C32, C42, C43, and C44 are directly supported by experimental data using 2-BP treatment (Figure 1F-G) and Cys-130 mutation (Figure 1H-I), with appropriate controls showing no effect on PI4P levels (C34, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or Golgi integrity (C35, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-E). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence strongly supports this result.

results.result: A series of hydrophobic residues (I113, W117, L120, L121, L124) within helix115-125 act in conjunction with the PB region to facilitate Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment. These residues align along a single face of the helix and are essential for NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C45, C46, C64, and C65 are supported by mutagenesis experiments (NLRP3HF mutant) showing that mutation of these hydrophobic residues abolishes Golgi recruitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C-D) and prevents response to ZDHHC overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D). Structural analysis (C31, Figure 1E) confirms the spatial arrangement of these residues.

results.result: The NLRP3 polybasic region (residues 131-158) alone is insufficient for Golgi localization but can direct membrane binding when paired with a second membrane-binding signal. Addition of a farnesylation motif (CVIM) to minimal NLRP3 constructs containing helix115-125, Cys-130, and the PB region achieves Golgi enrichment comparable to full-length NLRP3.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 and C47-C50 are supported by systematic analysis of minimal NLRP3 constructs (Figure 1B-C). The data show that GFP-NLRP3131-158 localizes to the nucleus (C27), while addition of CVIM redirects it to the plasma membrane (C28), and NLRP395-158-CVIM achieves Golgi localization (C49). This demonstrates the requirement for multiple membrane-binding elements working together.

results.result: The LRR domain (residues 731-1036) is important for optimal NLRP3 Golgi association, while the PYD domain (residues 1-95) is dispensable. Truncation analysis defines a minimal Golgi-binding region spanning residues 95-699.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by systematic truncation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 8). Removal of the PYD has no effect (C51, C57), while removal of the LRR reduces Golgi binding (C53, C56), and NLRP395-699 behaves similarly to NLRP31-699 (C55). The data consistently demonstrate the differential contributions of these domains.

results.result: Overexpression of specific ZDHHC palmitoyl-acyltransferases, particularly ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7, markedly enhances NLRP3 recruitment to the Golgi in a catalytic activity-dependent manner. ZDHHC5 overexpression redirects NLRP3 to the plasma membrane. These effects require both Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues in helix115-125.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 are supported by comprehensive ZDHHC overexpression experiments (Figure 2A-G). The data show differential effects of various ZDHHCs (C58-C62), dependence on catalytic activity (C63, Figure 2E-F), and requirement for Cys-130 and helix115-125 (C64-C65, Figure 2C, G). The convergence of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports this result.

results.result: Helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of membrane interaction independent of the polybasic region. Sensitivity to plasma membrane-localized ZDHHC5 requires an intact PB region, while cis-Golgi localized ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 even when the PB region is mutated.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by experiments with PB region mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D). The differential sensitivity to ZDHHC5 versus ZDHHC3 when the PB region is mutated (C66-C67) provides evidence for PB-independent membrane interaction (C68), though this interaction is insufficient for visible enrichment without additional signals.

results.result: In THP-1 macrophages, endogenous NLRP3 localizes to the perinuclear Golgi region in a manner dependent on Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues. Overexpression of catalytically active ZDHHC3 enhances both Golgi recruitment and nigericin-induced cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by experiments in THP-1 cells (Figure 3). Endogenous NLRP3 shows perinuclear localization (C69, Figure 3A), which is lost upon mutation of Cys-130 or hydrophobic residues (C70-C71, Figure 3B-C). ZDHHC3 overexpression enhances both Golgi recruitment (C72, Figure 3E) and cell death (C73-C74, Figure 3F-G) in a catalytic activity-dependent manner.

results.result: NLRP3 can be S-acylated at Cys-130, as demonstrated by PEG-switch assays. Full-length NLRP3 shows multiple S-acylation species, and ZDHHC3 overexpression or nigericin treatment increases singly S-acylated NLRP3 in a Cys-130-dependent manner. Minimal NLRP3 constructs (NLRP395-158) show Cys-130-dependent S-acylation only upon ZDHHC3 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C83 are supported by PEG-switch assays (Figure 4). The presence of multiple S-acylation bands (C75), changes upon Cys-130 mutation (C77), and correlation with ZDHHC3 overexpression/nigericin treatment (C78-C79) are all demonstrated. The minimal construct experiments (C80-C83, Figure 4E-G) provide direct evidence for Cys-130 S-acylation. However, the interpretation of multiple bands is somewhat uncertain given the presence of other S-acylated cysteines.

results.result: NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle involving both acylation and de-acylation. Treatment with the thioesterase inhibitor PalmostatinB or overexpression of the Golgi-localized thioesterase APT2 (but not mitochondrial APT1) affects NLRP3 Golgi localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C92 are supported by experiments with PalmostatinB (Figure 5A, C) and APT2 overexpression (Figure 5B, D). PalmostatinB causes loss of NLRP3 from the Golgi and redistribution to other compartments (C84-C85), while APT2 (but not APT1) overexpression reduces Golgi localization (C86-C87). The mitochondrial re-routing experiment (C91, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-G) demonstrates the acute effect of APT2. Together, these data support a dynamic S-acylation cycle (C92).

results.result: NLRP3 rapidly cycles on and off the Golgi with kinetics similar to mono-S-acylated N-Ras (half-time ~58 s). Nigericin treatment suppresses fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and increases the immobile fraction of NLRP3, indicating that NLRP3 becomes immobilized on the Golgi following activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by FRAP experiments (Figure 5E-G) and mitochondrial re-routing assays (Figure 5H-I). The FRAP data show rapid recovery in untreated cells (C93) and reduced recovery after nigericin treatment (C94-C95), with quantification of mobile and immobile fractions (Figure 5G). The mitochondrial re-routing data (C96) provide independent confirmation of reduced NLRP3 mobility after nigericin treatment.

results.result: Following nigericin treatment, NLRP3 becomes immobilized on the Golgi through reduced de-acylation of its Cys-130 lipid anchor. This is associated with segregation of NLRP3 from the Golgi-localized thioesterase APT2.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C99-C101 are supported by imaging data showing that APT2 and NLRP3 are closely opposed in untreated cells (C99, Figure 6A-B) but become segregated after nigericin treatment (C100-C101). This segregation, combined with the FRAP data showing reduced NLRP3 mobility (claims C94-C95), supports the conclusion that NLRP3 becomes immobilized through reduced de-acylation (C5).

results.result: Nigericin induces a breakdown in Golgi organization and function, causing dissociation of TGN and trans-Golgi membranes from cis/medial-Golgi and impairing secretory trafficking. This disruption leads to accumulation of cargo in cis/medial-Golgi compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C102-C107 are supported by imaging data showing Golgi disorganization (Figure 6C-D) and FM4-hGH trafficking assays (Figure 6C, D, F). The data demonstrate dissociation of TGN46 (C102) and p230 (C103) from cis/medial-Golgi, and impaired trafficking with cargo accumulation in STX5-positive compartments (C105-C107). These observations support the conclusion of nigericin-induced Golgi dysfunction (C6, C104).

results.result: Disruptions in Golgi homeostasis caused by nigericin are conveyed to NLRP3 through its acylation state. The nigericin-induced breakdown in Golgi organization may limit the ability of APT2 to encounter and de-acylate NLRP3.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C108 represent the authors' mechanistic interpretation linking Golgi disruption to NLRP3 immobilization. This is supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) nigericin causes Golgi disorganization (C102-C107), (2) NLRP3 becomes immobilized (C94-C95), (3) NLRP3 segregates from APT2 (C100-C101), and (4) NLRP3 immobilization is dependent on S-acylation at Cys-130 (C5, C42-C44). The mechanistic link is inferential but well-supported by the data.

results.result: Treatment with monensin, which does not activate NLRP3, also causes NLRP3 accumulation on the Golgi and impairs Golgi function. This demonstrates that enhanced Golgi recruitment alone is insufficient for NLRP3 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H) and FM4-hGH trafficking assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G). The observation that monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (C110, supported by citations), causes similar Golgi accumulation (C109) and dysfunction (C111) as nigericin provides an important control demonstrating that Golgi recruitment is necessary but not sufficient for activation.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 drive initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring provided by S-acylation at Cys-130. These three elements form a conserved functional unit essential for Golgi localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 represent the authors' mechanistic model synthesizing their experimental findings. This model is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) the PB region alone is insufficient (C27, C112), (2) all three elements are required for Golgi binding (C50, C115), (3) mutation of any element abolishes Golgi localization (C43-C46), and (4) the model is consistent with known mechanisms for other S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins (C113, supported by citations).

results.result: The authors speculate that LRR-dependent formation of an oligomeric NLRP3 complex may increase affinity for intracellular membranes through an avidity-based effect dependent on multiple monomers working together.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is speculative and based on inference from the observation that the LRR domain enhances Golgi binding (C53, C56) and structural data showing organization of polybasic regions around Cys-130 in oligomeric structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G). While plausible, this hypothesis is not directly tested and would require additional experiments (e.g., testing oligomerization-deficient mutants) to be considered supported.

results.result: A recent preprint suggests that ZDHHC7 is responsible for NLRP3 S-acylation at Cys-130 in macrophages, based on knockout experiments showing loss of Golgi localization and reduced activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by citation to a recent preprint (Yu et al., 2023). While the authors of the current manuscript did not perform these experiments themselves, the cited work provides independent validation of their findings regarding the importance of ZDHHC-mediated S-acylation for NLRP3 function. The claim is appropriately attributed to the cited work.

results.result: The authors speculate that alterations in charged lipid levels on endosomes caused by NLRP3 stimuli could allow NLRP3 to visit endosomal membranes and be trapped there by an endosomally localized PAT.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is speculative, based on inference from prior work on endosomal lipid changes (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) and the authors' own data showing ZDHHC5-mediated plasma membrane recruitment. While the authors demonstrate that NLRP3 can be redirected to different compartments by differentially localized ZDHHCs (C62), they do not directly test endosomal recruitment or identify endosomal PATs. This hypothesis requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: The authors speculate that regulation of Golgi access through S-acylation at Cys-130 may be important for oligomer formation and that the steady-state balance of S-acylation/de-acylation may keep Golgi-localized NLRP3 below a critical threshold for activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are speculative, based on inference from the known importance of membrane binding for oligomer formation (supported by citations) and the authors' data on the S-acylation cycle. While the model is plausible and consistent with the data, it is not directly tested. Testing would require experiments examining oligomerization states under different S-acylation conditions or measuring critical thresholds for activation.

results.result: Prior work shows that deletion of helix115-125 and/or Cys-130 impairs NLRP3 activation in mice, while deletion of exon-3 (residues 95-134) in human NLRP3 delays but does not completely block activation. This suggests that S-acylation and Golgi binding may accelerate inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to agonists, but activation can occur without Golgi binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by citations to prior work (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021; Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023). The authors appropriately cite and interpret these studies, noting the differential effects in mouse versus human systems. The interpretation that Golgi binding may accelerate but is not absolutely required for activation (C124-C125) is a reasonable inference from the cited data, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about NLRP3, inflammasomes, membrane binding mechanisms, S-acylation, and related proteins (K-Ras, H-Ras, N-Ras, APT2).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C26, C33, C36, C38, and C98 represent background information supported by citations to prior work. These claims establish the scientific context for the current study and are appropriately attributed to the cited literature. They are not novel findings of this manuscript but provide essential background for interpreting the results.

results.result: Nigericin treatment increases NLRP3 signal in the perinuclear area, and this accumulation is sensitive to BFA treatment and dependent on S-acylation (as shown by 2-BP treatment).
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C39-C41 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C for C37; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-D for C39-C40; Figure 1F-G for C41). These observations confirm prior reports of nigericin-induced NLRP3 recruitment and demonstrate its dependence on Golgi integrity (BFA sensitivity) and S-acylation (2-BP sensitivity).

results.result: The authors demonstrate that membrane association of NLRP3 is critically dependent on S-acylation of Cys-130, which traps NLRP3 in a dynamic S-acylation cycle at the Golgi. This is shown through 2-BP treatment experiments that inhibit Golgi enrichment of NLRP3, and mutation of Cys-130 that prevents Golgi enrichment at steady state and in response to nigericin treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that 'Cys-130 does seem to play a previously unappreciated role in membrane association of NLRP3,' but note that 'the evidence for S-acylation at Cys-130 is largely indirect.' The editor states that 'further work will be needed to clarify the details of the mechanism,' indicating acceptance of the role of Cys-130 but uncertainty about the mechanistic details.

results.result: The authors show that a series of hydrophobic residues (I113, W117, L120, L124) preceding Cys-130 act in conjunction with the PB region to facilitate Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment. Mutation of these hydrophobic residues abolishes recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at steady state and in response to nigericin.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly challenge these findings. The editor's statement that 'Cys-130 does seem to play a previously unappreciated role in membrane association' implicitly includes the supporting role of hydrophobic residues, as these are presented as part of the same functional unit. No concerns are raised about the mutagenesis data.

results.result: The authors propose that nigericin induces a breakdown in Golgi organization and function, causing segregation of NLRP3 from Golgi-localized thioesterase enzymes (APT2), which leads to NLRP3 becoming immobilized on the Golgi through reduced de-acylation of its Cys-130 lipid anchor. This is supported by FRAP experiments showing reduced NLRP3 mobility after nigericin treatment, segregation of NLRP3 from APT2, Golgi disorganization, and impaired secretory trafficking.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the process by which nigericin enhances membrane association is not yet fully understood.' While the data showing Golgi disruption and NLRP3 immobilization are acknowledged, the mechanistic link between these observations and the proposed segregation from thioesterases is not explicitly validated by reviewers.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that overexpression of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 markedly enhances recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi in a catalytically-dependent manner, and that ZDHHC3 overexpression enhances NLRP3-dependent cell death in THP-1 cells following nigericin treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the ZDHHC overexpression experiments. The editor's statement that the paper 'provides convincing evidence that S-acylation plays a key role in response to the stress induced by nigericin treatment' implicitly supports these findings, as ZDHHC enzymes catalyze S-acylation.

results.result: The authors use PEG-switch assays to show that NLRP3 can be S-acylated, revealing singly and doubly S-acylated species. They find that mutation of Cys-130 leads to only subtle changes in the S-acylation profile, and that enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding correlates with increased singly S-acylated NLRP3 species in a Cys-130 dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the evidence for S-acylation at Cys-130 is largely indirect.' The PEG-switch assay data showing subtle changes upon Cys-130 mutation and the presence of doubly S-acylated species even in the C130S mutant suggest complexity that is not fully resolved, contributing to reviewer uncertainty about the direct S-acylation of Cys-130.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle, as shown by the effects of PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression on NLRP3 localization, and by FRAP experiments showing kinetics similar to mono-S-acylated N-Ras.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the evidence for a dynamic S-acylation cycle. The editor states that the paper 'provides convincing evidence that S-acylation plays a key role,' which encompasses the dynamic cycling demonstrated by FRAP and thioesterase manipulation experiments.

results.result: The authors show that the NLRP3 polybasic region alone is insufficient to achieve Golgi localization, but can act in conjunction with a second membrane binding signal (such as farnesylation) to confer binding to specific intracellular membranes. They demonstrate that helix115-125, Cys-130, and the polybasic region are all essential for Golgi localization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings. The statement that 'Cys-130 does seem to play a previously unappreciated role in membrane association' implicitly acknowledges that the polybasic region alone is insufficient, as the authors demonstrate through their construct experiments.

results.result: The authors show through truncation experiments that the PYD domain is dispensable for NLRP3 Golgi association, while the LRR domain is important for optimal association. Truncation to residue 121 or 680 prevents or largely abolishes NLRP3 Golgi enrichment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these truncation experiments. These findings are presented as supporting data for the main conclusions about the membrane-binding determinants and are not questioned in the reviews.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that endogenous NLRP3 in THP-1 cells localizes to the perinuclear region where it partially overlaps with the trans-Golgi marker p230, and that mutation of Cys-130 or hydrophobic residues removes this perinuclear pool.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the endogenous NLRP3 localization data in THP-1 cells. These findings are consistent with the overexpression data and support the main conclusions about Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues.

results.result: The authors show that nigericin treatment increases NLRP3 signal within the perinuclear area, and that the membranes NLRP3 resides on post-stimulation are likely derived from the Golgi, as demonstrated by sensitivity to Brefeldin A treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations. The editor notes that the paper 'provides convincing evidence that S-acylation plays a key role in response to the stress induced by nigericin treatment,' which implicitly accepts the nigericin-induced changes in NLRP3 localization.

results.result: The authors show that sensitivity to plasma membrane-localized ZDHHC5 requires an intact PB region, while cis-Golgi localized ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 when the PB region is mutated, suggesting that helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of membrane interaction independent of the polybasic region.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings. These experiments provide mechanistic insight into how different ZDHHC enzymes can recruit NLRP3 to different membranes and are not challenged in the reviews.

results.result: The authors show that monensin, which does not activate NLRP3, also causes NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi and impairs Golgi function, suggesting that enhanced Golgi recruitment alone is insufficient for NLRP3 activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. This result provides important context for interpreting the nigericin data and is not questioned in the reviews.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring to Golgi membranes provided by S-acylation at Cys-130. They conclude that Cys-130, helix115-125, and the polybasic region form a highly conserved functional unit essential for NLRP3 Golgi localization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this model. The editor states that 'Cys-130 does seem to play a previously unappreciated role in membrane association of NLRP3,' which supports the proposed functional unit. The model is consistent with the experimental data presented.

comparisons.comparison: Both address Cys-130's role in membrane association (C2, C3, C32-C35, C42-C44). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by pharmacological and genetic evidence, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, acknowledging Cys-130's role but noting 'evidence for S-acylation at Cys-130 is largely indirect' and stating 'further work will be needed to clarify the details of the mechanism.'

Both evaluate hydrophobic residues and their role in Golgi recruitment (C4, C31, C45-C46, C64-C65). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not challenge the mutagenesis data, and the editor's acceptance of Cys-130's role implicitly includes these supporting residues.

Both address minimal construct experiments showing requirement for multiple membrane-binding elements (C27-C29, C47-C50, C112). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers acknowledge that polybasic region alone is insufficient, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of the systematic construct analysis.

Both evaluate truncation analysis showing differential domain contributions (C51-C57). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings, which serve as supporting data for membrane-binding determinants.

Both address ZDHHC overexpression experiments (C58-C65, with overlap on C58-C63). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on comprehensive experimental evidence. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with editor stating the paper 'provides convincing evidence that S-acylation plays a key role,' implicitly accepting ZDHHC enzyme data.

Both evaluate PB region mutants and differential ZDHHC sensitivity (C66-C68). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings showing PB-independent membrane interaction mechanisms.

Both address endogenous NLRP3 localization in THP-1 cells (C69-C71). OpenEval also includes ZDHHC3 effects (C72-C74). Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept the endogenous data as consistent with overexpression findings.

Both evaluate PEG-switch assay evidence for S-acylation (C75-C83). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED despite noting interpretation uncertainty. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'evidence for S-acylation at Cys-130 is largely indirect' and citing complexity from doubly S-acylated species in C130S mutant.

Both address dynamic S-acylation cycle evidence from PalmostatinB and APT2 experiments (C84-C93). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept the evidence for dynamic cycling, consistent with editor's statement about S-acylation's key role.

OpenEval R10 addresses FRAP experiments showing NLRP3 immobilization (C93-C97). Peer R3 addresses broader mechanistic claims about nigericin-induced immobilization and Golgi disruption (C5-C6, C94-C108). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'the process by which nigericin enhances membrane association is not yet fully understood.'

OpenEval R11 addresses APT2-NLRP3 segregation after nigericin (C5, C99-C101). Peer R3 includes this (C100-C101) within broader mechanistic uncertainty. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN regarding the mechanistic link between observations and proposed thioesterase segregation.

OpenEval R12 addresses Golgi disorganization and trafficking defects (C6, C102-C107). Peer R3 includes these claims (C102-C108) in broader mechanistic evaluation. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN about the mechanistic connection to NLRP3 immobilization despite acknowledging the observations.

OpenEval R13 addresses mechanistic interpretation linking Golgi disruption to NLRP3 immobilization (C7, C108). Peer R3 includes C108 in broader mechanistic uncertainty. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by convergent evidence; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN about the mechanistic process.

Both evaluate monensin control experiments (C109-C111). Both find claims SUPPORTED. This control demonstrates Golgi recruitment is necessary but not sufficient for activation, and peer reviewers do not challenge these findings.

Both address the mechanistic model for membrane-binding determinants (C112-C115). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept the model as consistent with experimental data showing all three elements are required.

Both address nigericin-induced NLRP3 recruitment and its dependencies (C37-C41). Both find claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept these observations as part of the convincing evidence for S-acylation's role in nigericin response.

OpenEval R16 addresses speculation about LRR domain enhancing avidity through oligomerization (C116). Rated UNCERTAIN by OpenEval as hypothesis not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval R17 addresses independent validation from Yu et al. 2023 preprint (C117). Rated SUPPORTED as appropriately cited work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval R18 addresses speculation about endosomal recruitment (C118). Rated UNCERTAIN as hypothesis requiring additional validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval R19 addresses speculation about S-acylation cycle and oligomerization thresholds (C119-C120). Rated UNCERTAIN as plausible but not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval R20 addresses interpretation of prior work on mouse vs human systems (C121-C125). Rated SUPPORTED based on appropriate citation and interpretation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval R21 addresses background information from prior literature (C1, C8-C26, C33, C36, C38, C98). Rated SUPPORTED as appropriately cited context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this background material.
